newsitem.title: CHINA: N.Koreans keep close watch on defector to South.
newsitem.headline: N.Koreans keep close watch on defector to South.

text.p: The highest-ranking North Korean to betray his Stalinist homeland began his fourth day marooned inside a South Korean embassy mission in Beijing on Saturday while North Koreans mounted a round-the-clock watch outside.

A North Korean delegation arrived in Beijing, but the identities of its members were unknown and it was unclear if they planned to discuss the defection of Hwang Jang-yop, who turned up at the mission on Wednesday with an aide.
Hwang has become the focus of a Cold War tussle between the two Koreas, arch-enemies since their 1950-53 war ended only in a truce.
China was playing for time as it agonised over a diplomatic quandary -- how to usher Hwang out of Beijing without offending its old socialist comrade or new capitalist friend.
Hwang, the scholarly architect of North Korea's national ideology of Juche, or self-reliance, was reported to be adamant he wanted to go to South Korea -- and nowhere else.
"I will die here if my determination to go to South Korea cannot be realised," Hwang said in a statement released by Seoul authorities.
"I want to make it clear that South Korea is the place where I want to go, and I will not go to any third country."
"He's very well, he's still in there and he's determined to go to (South) Korea," one South Korean embassy official said.

However, North Korean diplomats and students deployed on the fringes of a Chinese police cordon thrown around the Seoul mission in Beijing said they were convinced Hwang had been kidnapped and wanted to hear him speak up for himself.
"He is a very important person in our country," said one North Korean student among a group who said they had been told by the embassy to stake out the heavily-guarded mission.
"I want to know what happened," he said. "I am waiting for him to make an explanation.
"We just want a chance to see him," he said, denying that the North Koreans would use violent action to recover the man, who was a senior aide to North Korean leader Kim Jong-il.
Chinese police patrolling the sedate tree-lined streets in the diplomatic district around the mission appeared ready for a possible incident.
After North Korean diplomatic cars drove right up to police barricades on Friday night, police laid spikes across approaches to the building.

China has signalled its annoyance with South Korea's loudhailer diplomacy, and a flurry of diplomatic activity on Friday in Singapore, where Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen was attending Asia-Europe talks, failed to break the deadlock.
Ryu Kwang-sok, director-general of Asia-Pacific Affairs Bureau at Seoul's Foreign Ministry, said China wanted a low-key approach to resolving the crisis.
"I have the impression that China wants to resolve the row with Hwang quietly," he said.
China has appealed for calm and warned that it may take some time to decide what to do with Hwang.
"It can't be solved so quickly as imagined," Chinese spokesman Guo Chongli told reporters in Singapore on Friday.
Seoul sees the highest-level defection from the Stalinist North as a major coup that could produce a treasure trove of intelligence on a secretive government it fears is plotting its destruction.

It is a slap in the face for Pyongyang's top leader Kim Jong-il, whose 55th birthday party on Sunday was intended to smooth the way for his formal accession to the posts of state president and general secretary of the ruling Worker's Party.
South and North Korea were separated at the end of World War Two and fought a war from 1950 to 1953 which ended with a truce, not a peace treaty. China fought on North Korea's side in the conflict.
